segments.en: Kushe! How di bodi? That's how you say hello and how are you in Krio, the language almost everyone in Sierra Leone can speak. And the answer, with a smile, is often bodi fine, meaning I'm well.

More than five hundred years ago, Portuguese sailors saw the mountains rising behind this coast and named them Serra Leoa, the Lion Mountains. Some say the thunder rolling over the hills sounded like roaring lions.

Sierra Leone lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. Its capital, Freetown, climbs up green hills above one of the largest natural harbours in the world, with houses painted in every colour stacked up the slopes.

The name Freetown tells a story. In the late seventeen hundreds, formerly enslaved people from Britain, North America and the Caribbean came here to build new lives in freedom. Their descendants, the Krio people, gave the country its common language.
Many other peoples call Sierra Leone home too, including the Mende, the Temne, the Limba and the Kono, each with their own languages and traditions of music, masks and storytelling.
People here are proud of living side by side in peace across faiths. It's common for Muslim and Christian families to celebrate each other's festivals, and even to share the same household.

Now, food. Try cassava leaf stew, made from pounded leaves cooked with palm oil, fish or meat and hot pepper, served over rice. Groundnut soup, made with peanuts, is another favourite. People often say if you haven't eaten rice today, you haven't really eaten.
South of Freetown, the Freetown Peninsula has golden beaches fringed with palm trees, like River Number Two, where a river meets the sea, and the quiet Banana Islands just offshore.

Inland, rainforests are home to chimpanzees, colourful monkeys and the shy pygmy hippopotamus. On Tiwai Island, in the Moa River, you can walk through the forest at dawn and listen to the calls of the monkeys waking up.
Look for gara cloth, tie-dyed fabric in deep indigo blues and bright patterns, worn with pride at weddings and celebrations, and often tailored into flowing outfits.
Music fills the streets, from traditional drums and the balangi, a wooden xylophone, to modern Afropop blasting from taxis.
And football is a national passion. When the national team, the Leone Stars, play, the whole country seems to stop to watch.
Tenki, thank you, for coming to visit. Head north across the border, and Guinea, with its high green hills where great rivers begin, is waiting for you.
